claims.text: Controlled heat treatment can induce nanoscale precipitation in a high-entropy alloy.
A moderate density of nanoscale precipitates impedes dislocation motion.
Dislocation impediment by a moderate precipitate density delays crack initiation.
Overexposure during heat treatment produces an excessive precipitate density.
An excessive precipitate density embrittles the alloy and reduces toughness.
The initial material is a single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloy with minimal or no nanoscale precipitates.
A suitable temperature-time regime can form fine, coherent nanoscale precipitates without significant grain growth or phase instability.
Nanoscale precipitates increase the energy barrier for crack initiation and propagation.
An optimal precipitate density enhances toughness.
An excessive precipitate volume fraction causes embrittlement by excessively hindering dislocation glide.
Optimally heat-treated samples will have greater toughness than the untreated single-phase alloy.
Samples with excessive precipitate density will have lower toughness than both optimally treated and untreated samples.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to high-entropy alloys with moderate lattice distortion that form coherent or semi-coherent nanoscale precipitates.
The hypothesis may not apply to alloys with extreme compositional or structural instability.
The hypothesis may not apply under temperature regimes that cause phase coarsening or additional transformation mechanisms.
